title: The Cliff Effect in a Multi-User OFDM Hybrid Beamforming Downlink: The Cyclic Prefix and Design Trade-Offs
content: Millimeter-wave orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) uses a short cyclic prefix designed for small cells, yet future deployments may extend these links toward 1 km. Coded digital links fail abruptly once the channel can no longer support the selected rate, a behavior known as the cliff effect. This paper characterizes the cliff in an OFDM-based multi-user hybrid beamforming downlink at 28 GHz with joint spatial division and multiplexing (JSDM), and traces it to its cause. User groups are placed from 400 to 1000 m in a non-line-of-sight channel whose scatterers surround each user. Monte Carlo simulations of 50 realizations vary the cyclic prefix length, the number of base station antennas and the modulation order. Block error rate, goodput, bit error rate, error vector magnitude and the maximum per-subcarrier condition number are reported for every user. With a 0.64 µs prefix, users up to 600 m are error-free, users at 800 m lose 6–8% of their frames and users at 1000 m 62–66%. The cliff begins just before the maximum excess delay of the channel reaches the prefix length. A sweep from 32 to 128 samples moves it as this ratio predicts, and the rise of the condition number at the cell edge disappears once the prefix is long enough. Cell goodput peaks with an 80-sample prefix, 14% above the baseline. Arrays of 128 to 512 antennas leave the cliff unchanged, which rules out a spatial cause. A higher modulation order loses more frames at 800 and 1000 m without moving the cliff, yet delivers more goodput up to 800 m and less at 1000 m.
